passage: I'm Tenzin, and last month I tried something new. Raghav and I were on the hostel roof after exams, and he asked how things were at home since my parents separated. Normally I'd say "fine" and find a reason to leave. I felt that exact pull, my hand already on my phone. This time I said, "I want to leave right now. That's what I do when people ask." Raghav just nodded and waited. So I stayed. I told him one small thing: that I hadn't gone home at Diwali because the house feels too quiet now. That was all. He said, "Thanks for telling me," and passed me the chips. Nothing bad happened. The next week I told him a little more.

qa.q: Where were Tenzin and Raghav when Raghav asked about home?
qa.a: They were on the hostel roof after exams.

qa.q: What was Tenzin feeling when Raghav asked about home, and what shows it?
qa.a: Tenzin felt uncomfortable and wanted to escape; Tenzin's hand was already on the phone, ready to find a reason to leave.

qa.q: What turning point came on the roof, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Tenzin said the urge to leave out loud and stayed to share one small thing, and when nothing bad happened, sharing more became easier.

qa.q: How might Raghav have felt when Tenzin admitted wanting to leave?
qa.a: He may have felt trusted, and it helped him know to wait quietly instead of pushing.

grounding: A student notices the pull to withdraw, names it aloud, stays and shares one small truth with a safe friend, and finds it is met kindly.

passage:
Supervisor's note, Hansa, design studio internship.
Tushar, 21, usually goes silent in feedback meetings and leaves for "a call". Today, when the team asked what he found hard about the brief, he started gathering his sketches, then stopped. "I'm noticing I want to walk out," he said. "Give me a second." He stayed. He told us he'd been stuck for three days and hadn't asked because he hates needing help. Nobody made a fuss; Farida offered to pair with him. He stayed ten minutes past the meeting, sketching with her.
Next step: a quiet check-in with him on Friday, low-key, to keep the door open.

qa.q: How long had Tushar been stuck on the brief?
qa.a: He had been stuck for three days.

qa.q: Why had Tushar not asked for help before?
qa.a: He hates needing help, perhaps fearing it would make him look weak or bring a bad reaction.

qa.q: What choice did Tushar make when he wanted to walk out, and what came of it?
qa.a: He named the urge aloud, asked for a second and stayed to admit he was stuck, which led to Farida offering to pair with him.

qa.q: How might the team see Tushar after this meeting?
qa.a: They may find him more approachable, someone who will now say when he is stuck.

grounding: A supervisor notes an intern who names his urge to withdraw, stays past his comfort and shares a small need with a safe team.

passage:
Saturday night. Pallavi cried on the terrace tonight about her dad's surgery, and every muscle in me wanted to say I had an assignment and leave. Instead I said it out loud: "I've got the urge to run right now. It's not you. I'm just bad at this." She laughed through her tears. I stayed twenty more minutes, which felt like two hours. Then, weirdly, I told her something I've never told anyone here: I hate my birthday because nobody at home ever remembered it. She didn't make a big deal. She just said, "Noted. I'll remember." Nothing bad happened. I'm writing this down so I believe it tomorrow.
Lakshmi

qa.q: How much longer did Lakshmi stay on the terrace?
qa.a: Twenty more minutes.

qa.q: What was Lakshmi feeling while Pallavi cried?
qa.a: Lakshmi felt a strong urge to flee and was uneasy with the closeness, but chose to name it and stay.

qa.q: Which step worked, and why?
qa.a: Saying the urge to run out loud, because it let Lakshmi stay without pretending and made a small honest disclosure possible.

qa.q: How might Pallavi feel hearing about the birthday?
qa.a: Pallavi probably feels trusted and touched, and her simple "I'll remember" shows she welcomes the need.

grounding: Shows an avoidant young adult naming the urge to withdraw, staying longer and making a small disclosure that is met kindly.

passage: At the Pushkar fair ground, Hansa bought two cups of chai and asked, "Aditi, why do you never talk about home?" Aditi felt the familiar pull: say "nothing to tell" and go and find the bus. She looked at the camel carts instead. Then she said, "I want to change the subject right now. I'm noticing that." Hansa waited, blowing on her tea. Aditi stayed, though her hands were cold. "My father left when I was eight. I've told nobody here." Hansa didn't gasp or grab her. She just nodded. "Thank you for telling me." They watched the lamps come on over the lake. Aditi's shoulders came down a little. On the bus back she messaged Hansa: "Same time next week?"

qa.q: Where did Hansa and Aditi drink chai?
qa.a: At the Pushkar fair ground.

qa.q: What was Aditi feeling when Hansa asked about home?
qa.a: She felt the familiar pull to escape and was nervous, with cold hands, yet chose to stay.

qa.q: What made it easier for Aditi to open up?
qa.a: Naming the urge aloud and Hansa's calm, patient response with no big reaction.

qa.q: How might Hansa see the message on the bus?
qa.a: Hansa probably feels glad and trusted, since Aditi wants to meet again after sharing something hard.

grounding: Shows a young adult who notices the urge to withdraw, says so, stays and makes a small disclosure to a safe friend.

passage:
Leila and Emeka were washing up after dinner in their shared house in Leeds when Emeka said, "You've seemed low since your gran's call. Want to talk about it?"
Leila felt the familiar urge to say "I'm fine" and go upstairs. Her hands tightened on the plate.
Instead she said, "I want to run to my room right now. That's what I usually do."
Emeka kept drying. "You can. Or you can stay."
She stayed, leaning against the counter. It took a long minute. "Gran's ill, and I haven't visited since Christmas. I feel guilty, and I hate saying it."
"That sounds heavy," Emeka said. He didn't lecture or fix. He just made two cups of tea.
Later, in her room, Leila noticed she felt lighter, not smaller, for having said it.

qa.q: Where did Leila and Emeka live?
qa.a: In their shared house in Leeds.

qa.q: What did Leila feel when Emeka asked about the call?
qa.a: She felt the familiar urge to withdraw, tense enough that her hands tightened on the plate, and underneath she felt guilty about her gran.

qa.q: Which of Leila's choices helped her, and why?
qa.a: She named the urge to run aloud and stayed a little longer, sharing one honest thing, which showed her that need did not bring rejection.

qa.q: How might Emeka see Leila's decision to stay?
qa.a: Emeka probably felt trusted, and chose to listen and make tea rather than lecture, which made it safe for her.

grounding: Shows a young adult noticing the urge to withdraw, saying it aloud, staying longer and learning that a small disclosure is met with care.
